name: Chiapas
summary_text: Same-sex conduct is legal and no law targets trans presence, but Chiapas is one of six states whose legislature has refused to create any legal gender recognition procedure (Human Rights Watch, March 2025). The practical consequence is permanently mismatched identity documents for trans people - the single most visitor-relevant legal fact in Mexico, since document mismatch is what triggers questioning at checkpoints - with no local procedure to cure it; courts can order recognition case by case, and Chiapas' proximity to Tabasco (where HRW documented mistreatment of trans people in state institutions) indicates a conservative institutional climate. Worse than the national position on documents and machinery, with no dedicated violence signal of its own.

sources.title: Trans Rights in Mexico: Progress and Challenges | Human Rights Watch
sources.claim_summary: Human Rights Watch state-by-state tracker on legal gender recognition in Mexico (March 2025), covering which of the 32 states have legislated an administrative procedure and the Supreme Court rulings that drove expansion. Lists Chiapas among the ten of 32 states that had NOT reformed legislation to create a legal gender recognition procedure as of March 2025.

sources.title: “I Just Want to Contribute to Society”: The Need for Legal Gender Recognition in Tabasco, Mexico | HRW
sources.claim_summary: Human Rights Watch report 'I Just Want to Contribute to Society' (6 March 2024) on Tabasco: no legal gender recognition procedure there exposes trans people to institutional mistreatment - the August 2023 killing of activist Karina Gomez remained unsolved, hate-motivation provisions are absent from Tabasco's criminal code, and healthcare staff routinely out patients by calling legal names. Baseline for how a non-reforming state behaves.

sources.title: Transfemicide becomes a crime in a ‘watershed’ moment for Mexico City | Transgender | The Guardian
sources.claim_summary: Guardian report (24 July 2024) on Mexico City making transfemicide a crime with sentences up to 70 years (the 'Paola Buenrostro law', approved 18 July 2024), in one of Latin America's deadliest settings for trans people; over 95% of homicides nationally went unpunished in 2022.
